Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization he had made it possible for Bismark to develop his program, and the United States apparently had the wisdom in those days to listen to this great authority. Partly as a result she has since had a determination to sell her surplus goods abroad, no matter what the difficulties might appear to be. With generations of tradition in favour of such a policy, what chance, I ask you, would even a dozen Canadian ministers of finance have of moving the United States authorities from this traditional policy to any serious degree.
The United States has used her economic power to compel other nations to buy her goods. How does she do it? This is a most rewarding study. It certainly does not leave one with the admiration for the United States which one had before engaging in that study. Her present policy began with Woodrow Wilson's 14 points particularly No. 3; it was followed up by the most favoured nation clause, reinforced in time by the unconditional most favoured nation clause adopted in 1922. The policy has been developed since then, and has resulted in such monstrosities as GATT which too many Canadians seem to think is a kind of instrument of our salvation. In fact, GATT was contrived by the United States and forced upon the rest of the nations by the United States in order to enable her to drive her goods into the economy of almost any nation under the sun.
That may seem extreme. It would be good to see an agricultural committee sinking its teeth into such a problem with genuine authorities to guide it. Hon. members sitting on that committee would then find that what I have said is true. The United States is determined to maintain employment, that is, to export her unemployment, regardless of the cost to other nations. In the course of a speech made in October, 1944, President Roosevelt declared: "I intend to find jobs for 60 million Americans by trebling our exports abroad". That was the thinking which was prevailing in the United States during the second world war, and it is prevailing there still.
We should probe into the possibilities of commonwealth co-operation enabling the nations of the commonwealth to help to protect the economies of the various members of this great family; and if the commonwealth is unable to do this we must find out why. All these matters would have a tremendous bearing on the policies we would undertake to adopt in respect of Canadian agriculture.
Another problem which needs to be studied with great care is to what extent are our surpluses the result of low prices rather than
[Mr. Blaekmore.l

of high prices. This matter has been mentioned once or twice by speakers who have preceded me today. If low prices do bring about surpluses, then the minister, with all his good intentions, could probably be defeating his own ends. That would be too bad. I am convinced it would help him very much if he could have the benefit of advice from an agricultural committee which could go into the whole question appertaining to this matter.
Another problem is to what extent would it seem advisable to encourage the large farm rather than the family size of farm. Naturally, all of us favour the family sized farm. I do. But before we adapt our policy to the protection of the family size of farm we really ought to go into the matter of whether we are endeavouring through our agricultural economy to produce wheat and other products as cheaply as possible or to produce farm people, and the decision would have to be made after careful consideration and after discussions in which the farm people of Canada as well as the urban people should participate. As far as I can judge, the only place where we could have a dispassionate consideration and study of all these various problems is the committee on agriculture and colonization.
The minister will feel that he is in duty bound to take measures in fulfilment of the promises which his party has made. I recognize that, but I think the minister will also realize that he is just as much in duty bound to do the right thing when he does take action and not adopt policies which might, without it being his intention and without it being his fault, actually make matters worse.
So far as I and the members of my party can judge, after giving this whole question careful consideration, it would appear that the Agricultural Prices Support Act which the Liberal administration adopted in 1944 is capable of being used to benefit the farmers quite as much as is the bill which the minister now proposes, even if he puts into it all the amendments which may be required in order to try to meet the demands of those who are talking to him and besetting him to the point where I marvel he has not already gone distracted. Having all this in mind, I should say it does not really make very much difference whether this bill is put on the statute books today or tomorrow or some little time hence, because if it is not put on the statute books the Agricultural Prices Support Act will still be there. The minister, by using vision, courage and originality, will be able to use that act to bring into effect all the good things which he has in his heart and mind.

I repeat again that I propose to support the motion to refer this present bill to the committee on agriculture and colonization, and I also point out once more that the bill as it stands at the present time is completely unacceptable to Social Crediters.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on Bill No. 237, the agricultural stabilization bill, I am speaking for the first time in this renowned and time-honoured chamber. I should like immediately to join with those speakers who have preceded me in congratulating the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker on their elevation to the Speaker's chair. As this session of parliament has progressed it has become extremely evident that those appointments were well and justly made.
Like the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Doucett), the hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) and our newest member from the Yukon-although he is not in his seat as yet, many of us have had the pleasure of meeting him and are looking forward to the great contribution he will undoubtedly make to this house-I am one of the youngest members of this house with respect to the number of months of service to his constituency since June 10. By that I mean the election in my riding of Wellington South was a deferred election held on July 15 due to the untimely death of the late Henry Hosking the Liberal candidate and former member of this house.
At this time, Mr. Speaker, I would like to pay my respects to Mr. Hosking and I am sure hon. gentlemen on the other side of the house who knew him well will join me in this tribute. Mr. Hosking and I met on common ground on many occasions and, although we shared opposing political views, I respected him for his very arduous and diligent attention to the interests of the constituents of the riding I now represent. He devoted his talents, his time and his efforts to his riding in the same way as many of us are doing now.
I am particularly happy to take part in the debate on this agricultural bill because the riding I represent has long been known for its many contributions to the field of agriculture and, I might add, to the field of politics as well. In proof of this statement I need only to mention the late hon. Hugh Guthrie, leader of the opposition and for many years minister of justice in this house, the late R. W. Gladstone, a distinguished senator, and the Right Hon. George Drew, former premier of Ontario, leader of the opposition in this house and now Canadian high commissioner to the United Kingdom.
Returning to the subject of agriculture, Mr. Speaker, I take pride in pointing out that it 96698-217
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization was to my riding that the first Hereford animal was imported to Canada by the late F. W. Stone in 1860, almost 100 years ago. The first Angus cow to be imported to Canada was brought to Guelph by the late James Bowman. The first Shorthorn cattle, although landed at St. Catharines, were very soon driven to Guelph and the breed was propagated there.
The Ontario Agricultural College and the Ontario Veterinary College, the largest universities of their kind in the British Empire, are situated in the centre of Wellington South at Guelph, Ontario. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, these facts coupled with the fact that the Ontario Agricultural College is my alma mater and I am a retail meat merchant and farmer explain my particular interest in this agricultural bill.
The introduction of this bill, I feel, is the result of several things. First, and I think most important, it is the result of the depressed condition in which the farmers of Canada found themselves when our party went to the country. What were the agricultural conditions which existed across this great country of ours? I cannot speak for all parts of Canada but I do know what conditions existed in my own riding. Many farms were run down in appearance and condition, the soil was being robbed, the farmers were living off their depreciation. Many farmers were carrying on a part-time operation, working part time in factories. Farmers' wives and children were required to work in order to help make ends meet. Implement dealers were unable to make sales. I could continue enumerating these conditions but all hon. members know the story.
Between 1946 and 1956 prices of commodities and services used by Canadian farmers rose by 58.2 per cent, between 1951 and 1956 prices of farm produce declined by 21.8 per cent. In 1956 the net income per Canadian family was $4,900 while the net income per farm family was $3,037. In other words, the farm family was being asked to live on $1,863 a year less than the average Canadian family, to accept a standard of living reduced by that amount. Turkeys were pouring into my riding from the United States. Cheese came in from New Zealand. Boat loads of lambs came in from New Zealand and Australia. Canned peaches came in from the United States. And while all this was going on, Liberal cabinet ministers were travelling around the country telling the farmers that they were never better off. The hon. member for Melville (Mr. Gardiner) told the turkey producers that they would have to accept less in order to meet United States competition. Mr. Speaker, did we

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization ever hear any members of the former government telling manufacturers of automobiles, furniture, appliances, boots, shoes and clothing that they should take less in order to meet United States' competition? No, they raise prices as they choose.
The then minister of finance, Walter Harris, in his speeches conveyed the idea that his government should allow agricultural products to come into Canada from the United States in order to keep our prices down. Hon. Milton F. Gregg once said in my riding, "Canada had the best year in her history; of course, farm income was down." The question of farm income was casually dismissed as though it were completely incidental.
I have outlined, Mr. Speaker, some of the conditions that the former Liberal government knew about and allowed to exist. The election came and after it was over the Conservative party formed the government. It was decided that something should be done- yes, something should be done immediately -to correct this unfair situation. We promised we would and we have. It is well known to all how quickly our government acted with respect to the importation of turkeys. Our present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) had not yet been appointed and was then only acting minister of agriculture when he put turkeys under price support and import control. Just speak to any turkey producer and ask him what he thinks of our party. Ask the dairy man, too; he knows about the import control on butter oil and powdered milk, etc.
We now have before us a bill that fulfils another promise we made to relieve the distressed condition of agriculture. This bill represents another proof to those people of the rural areas who gave us such wonderful support that our promises were sincere. I think the minister is to be commended on this bill, for his willingness to hear representations from farm organizations, and for his eagerness to get the viewpoints of his party backbenchers. In other words I am sure he feels that in order to be successful such a bill must have embodied in it the thinking and the suggestions of the man from the back concession. The fact that he has introduced amendments proves, without fear of contradiction, that he is willing to co-operate, assist and give sympathetic consideration to anything that will help agriculture. I have been amazed at the number of times I have heard farm delegates say when they have come to Ottawa to present their views, "There sure is a different attitude around here now".
This bill, for the first time, is going to give the farmer something to go by. It is going


to give him a chance to plan his program, to plan in advance. Some hon. members can debate and argue as they like but I feel that the old bill never did just that. Too much was left to the minister of agriculture. Support prices just seemed to be pulled out of the air. Nothing was said as to how long they would be in force. But now we have a formula, a flexible formula, a formula any farmer can use and go about his business with a sense of security and stability.
I support the bill because it is flexible, because it takes into consideration the law of supply and demand, something that is most important. The United States system of agricultural support has found that to be the case. They have had great difficulties, involving great surpluses and great cost to the treasury because they have more or less ignored the law of supply and demand.
The advisory committee that the bill calls for, composed of farmers and members of agricultural organizations, will, while setting the prescribed prices each year, likely in January, base their decisions chiefly on the supply and demand picture and they shall have regard to the estimated average cost of production as outlined in the legislation. I should like to repeat that because I think there are many who feel this aspect has not been taken into account. The bill distinctly says that they shall have regard to the estimated average cost of production as outlined in the act.
I should like to take a concrete example of how the bill will work. Suppose I want to feed a number of steers this year on a feed lot. From dominion bureau of statistics figures I can ascertain the average selling price for steers for the last 10 years. I add these prices, divide by 10 and arrive at the basic price which in this particular case is $21.80 a hundredweight. According to the legislation 1 know that the support price for the next 12 months could not be less than 80 per cent of the base price or $17.44 a hundredweight. However, on studying the supply and demand situation I could very likely estimate the prescribed price that would be set by the advisory board. Unless the supply was extremely heavy I would expect the price to settle somewhere around the 10-year average, namely $21.80. I would at least have some idea what I should pay for my stocker cattle, as close to $17.14 a hundred as possible.
In the case of hogs you could arrive at a similar price. You would take the average prices for the last 10 years, obtainable from the dominion bureau of statistics, add them and divide by 10 and you would find that the base price would be $29.08 and the support or drastic level price for 1958 should not be

under $23.26. As I said before, the advisory board should meet preferably in January and again in the fall, and after a close study of the supply and demand situation they would set the prescribed price close to today's level, namely 27 cents.
The agricultural prices stabilization bill is sound, comprehensive and courageous legislation. I do not believe the bill will correct all the ills of agriculture. It will no doubt need further amending from time to time. The government has acted-I repeat, the government has acted-as we promised we would. The success of the bill will depend upon sound judgment, a sense of fairness in the administration of the legislation and the utmost co-operation from the farm organizations to make it succeed.
The farmer on the back concession needs help. Give him a sound agricultural policy. Let the law of supply and demand work. Give him some protection from the dumping of agricultural products and he will work hard and produce the food we need. But let us give him at least an even break so he can have the standard of living which he justly deserves. I appreciate, Mr. Speaker, the privilege of speaking at this time in support of the bill. I sincerely hope it will be passed immediately so that its many benefits may reach the farmer whom we all know needs immediate help.

Mr. Speaker, I regret having to tell you and all the other hon. members that I am disappointed by the bill that the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) has just introduced to help the farmers, although it has been amended three times.
Only once.

I would have liked the bill to be introduced immediately after the adoption of the one about assistance to the western grain producers, because at that time I voted in favour of that legislation, in the hope that corresponding benefits would be offered to genuine farmers.
Unfortunately, we have waited with impatience for more than three months, and now we are faced with an offer that I consider, I think, at its real value. So. I regret to admit that instead of helping the farmers it will be detrimental to them.

Well, vote against it.

Mr. Speaker, I will not hold the Minister of Agriculture responsible for that. I know him very well and I think he is a good friend of mine. But I also feel that he has been subjected to the influence of his cabinet colleagues since there would seem to be no other way of explaining this disadvantageous project, which will contribute to a lowering of the support prices. He should have had something better to offer.
I understand that during the last campaign the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) went around the country making a lot of irresponsible promises. They felt sure that they would not be called upon to take office. Hence their present predicament. The resolution brought forward by the minister suggests the establishment of some form of parity price, but the experience I have gained, I think, over the forty years and more during which I have been in close contact with the farmers and during which I have been a member of every association, as well as the experience I have gained through fourteen years of farming 1,000 acres of good land, raising cattle, pigs and poultry, leads me to believe that if the farmer is to get a parity price for his products, these should fetch from 30 to 40 per cent more than they do now. I have reference here to those things produced by mixed farmers. This is not going to be the case if we are to go by the minister's offer. This will, I feel, bring about a price which will be from 10 to 15 per cent lower than the present price received by the farmer.
The mixed farmer finds himself in a difficult position. A great many of them leave the land. There are two main explanations for this, but in neither case does the fault lie with the former government. Twenty years ago a farmer who had 100 acres of land, some head of cattle and agricultural machinery, had costs amounting to approximately $15,000.
In those days, they were using horses and inexpensive farm machinery. Labour costs were 25 per cent of what they are now and so on. Nowadays, in these modern times, a farmer needs at least 150 to 250 acres of land and modern plowing equipment which has a total value of at least $30,000 to $35,000. He has to maintain his farm, his ditches, his fences, and his buildings. You know how many buildings are needed for various types of livestock:	pig-pens, hen-houses, barn,
stable, implement shed, garage, normal storage and freezing facilities, as well as the farmer's own living quarters. All that is worth at least $20,000 to $25,000. Therefore how can a young farmer get a loan to buy a hundred

Another reason why they leave the land are the attractive wages now paid to workers, and the short working hours, to which, in many cases, are added holidays and a pension plan. I am very happy that all our wage-earners should have them, but we must keep in mind that the farmer who has taken up mixed farming is a very useful citizen as he produces most of the commodities which we need for consumption; moreover, he is one of the main buyers of all sorts of manufactured products, iron fences, cement, fertilizers, machines of all kinds, equipment for stables, motors, shearing-machines, milking-machines, refrigerators, and so on, and he buys more clothing than anybody else since he works in the dirt, in bad weather, and must wear a different set of clothes at home in the evening and still others to go out. Like any other citizen, he needs a car and often a truck, perhaps even a car for his sons, since transportation is not as readily available to him as to city dwellers. He cannot find helpers since salaried people would not work 60 hours a week without unemployment insurance when they can work 40 hours a week with the benefit of unemployment insurance and, in many cases, with the benefit of a pension after a certain number of years. I do not blame these people; I would do the same thing in their place. Nevertheless, that is why people leave the farm.
The exodus of our farmers to the city cannot now continue at this rate for it could cause untold difficulties to industrial workers in the cities where many are now without work and shelter, thus decreasing the number of buyers for all the products mentioned-
Mr. Speaker, does the hon. member allow me a question?
You make your speech when your turn comes.
Why did my hon. friend refrain from speaking about this for the last 22 years?
He did better than that.
It does not show.
Mr. Speaker, I have been a member of this house for the past twelve years and I have never known a member to be so unfair to others and to interject remarks so devoid of intelligence.
That is probably because he was a member of the Liberal party.

As I was saying, this situation would reduce the number of buyers of products I mentioned a moment ago, besides reducing the number of buyers of western grain because farmers of Ontario, Quebec and the maritimes are good customers for the grain producers of the prairie provinces.
Now then, to remedy this situation as I see it, for the farmers of the provinces which I just mentioned, it would be necessary to raise immediately by at least fifteen per cent the guarantee of the base price, commonly called the floor price, which would mean 65 cents for butter, 45 cents for eggs, 28 cents for hogs and so on for the other products. The Liberal party passed an act along these lines in 1944 and improved it afterwards.
It would be better for the government to raise the base price of the farmer's products by 15 to 20 per cent of the present base price.
The guaranteed price on cheese could then be 34 cents a pound while the premium on bacon could be raised to $4. I also believe that the freight subsidy on western grain should be raised to $3 a ton and that our grain producers in Ontario should have the same guarantee as the grain producers of western Canada.
The government should also offer our farmers loans of at least 80 per cent of the actual value of the lands. It should see to it, either through an agreement or tariff regulations, that the commodities for which we guarantee a floor price, such as powdered milk, butter, cheese, and other products likely to compete with our farm products, are not shipped to Canada.
The government should also set up an advisory committee made up of consumers and farmers, as well as men with a good experience in large scale mixed farming.
I feel that the committee should have the authority to investigate the spread between the price the farmer gets for his products and the price paid by the consumers; for instance, for a piece of cheese which the consumers pay, as I do, 43 cents for half a pound,

or 86 cents a pound, the farmer receives only for that cheese a little under 30 cents. It's about the same for most agricultural products.
According to a bulletin entitled Dairy Facts *-the Farmer's Share of the Consumer's Dollar, butter yields to the farmers 77 per cent of the consumer's dollar, beef, 57 per cent, pork, 51 per cent, potatoes, 41 per cent, preserves, 24 per cent; and cheese, as I just said, 34 per cent.
I do not wish to commend the sending of a delegation to Great Britain to allow these people to sell us more products that we most likely make here, which will harm our industries and increase unemployment; we have enough of it. Incidentally, I thought it was extraordinary for the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) to say in the house, while boasting of his great success in British Columbia, to the effect that the federal government would pay $16,000 a month to a certain company so that it may keep 400 men on the job while 350 other workers of that company will get unemployment insurance benefits.
I think it might be preferable to have delegations, not of 50, but of 2 or 3 people who, with government representatives abroad, with our ambassadors, would go and sell our agricultural and industrial products to the various foreign countries. Industries might also send their representatives.
Here is a sample of flax fiber which in 1940 was selling for 32 cents in England, and in 1942 for 60 cents a pound in the United States. We made a sacrifice in order to sell this flax fiber to the United Kingdom for 32 cents a pound, and now they offer us 13 cents a pound, because they are buying it from Russia at 16J cents a pound, delivered in Scotland. This means that, if we were to sell it for 13 cents a pound, our farmers would earn 10 cents an hour for their labour, and our industrial workers would get from 15 to 20 cents an hour.
I have been chairman of the National Flax Board since it was founded in 1939, and it had to close down all its plants. Now we have 1,500 unemployed workers and Russia is laughing at us.
Will Mr. Speaker allow me to put a question to the hon. member?

The hon. member and his colleague who interrupted me a while ago, would make a fine pair together. I have been sitting in this house for twelve years and I have never met people who so little knew how to behave.

In any event, I put this suggestion in good faith in the best interests of every real farmer, as well as of Canadians in general.
In conclusion, I would ask my good friend the hon. Minister of Agriculture-he is one of my good friends and a nice fellow-to change the offers he has made so that his bill may be referred to the committee on agriculture and colonization-
Give us the figures for the years 1956 and 1957.

-so that all the representations of the farmer groups may be heard and the bill improved. I will support the bill, do not worry, since your Conservative colleagues, by the look of them and by their attitude, as far as I have been able to see from the expression on their faces, seemed as sorry as we did, in the opposition, when you brought your proposals forward. I could see on their faces that they were saying to themselves: Not one of us here representing agricultural constituencies will be re-elected at the next election.
(Text):
May I say this to my good friends and neighbours, the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott (Mr. Villeneuve) and the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) who is not here, who for many years were promising double prices for farmer's products, parity price, and so on, in my district and in their own districts: What are you doing now, my friends? Here is the place to fulfil your promises.
Give us time.
This is the time to have your government do something for the farmers, and get a fair floor price as I have asked.
Vote against it.
This is what the farmers want, so that they will know ahead at least what will be the lowest prices paid for their products.
You will vote for it anyway.

I hope that my friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) will get more help from these hon. members who represent farmers in order to get something better than what he has. I admire him, and I know that he is an honest gentleman.

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization

Mr. Speaker, in the beginning I should like to point out that to my way ot thinking it is rather unfortunate that we are obliged to continue to discuss this amendment which is no more than a simple and fair request. Surely there is nothing wrong with asking the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) to refer this agricultural price stabilization bill to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization for study before this house is called on to make a final decision. I assume that most members of the committee are well aware of the farm price problem. By putting their heads together surely they can figure out some appropriate recommendations and perhaps improve this legislation to the point where it will solve this problem. I can assure the minister that this bill, in its present form, does not even come close to curing the deep seated farm price problem.
Unlike other groups in Canadian society, Canadian agriculturalists have been unable to build and retain a strong, permanent educational and protective organization and maintain a position of "parity" with other groups. While other groups banded together for self-preservation, farmers followed the maxim of "every man for himself". Consequently these hard working, hard sweating and often financially hard pressed individualists suffered much from unfair competition resulting in a merciless cost-price squeeze which has now reached the point where, by and large, the vast majority of them are operating in the red and are facing imminent insolvency.
In a brief submitted by the Manitoba government to the royal commission on economic prospects, it has been proved that the gross income of Manitoba farmers decreased from $280.5 million in 1948 to $197.7 million in 1954. Their net income fell from $182.2 million in 1948 to $71.9 million in 1954 and their return per dollar of capital investment dropped from 18 per cent in 1948 to one-tenth of one per cent in 1954. This is as far as the deterioration had progressed three years ago. Today it is much worse.
Those who have an intimate knowledge of the farm situation are well aware of the fact that today agriculture has become the soft spot in our economy and that constructive measures must be taken on the government level to raise and stabilize farm prices if complete economic stagnation on the farm front, that may turn into a country-wide recession or even an over-all economic depression, is to be prevented. But in spite of the urgency of the situation and the fact that the Liberals professed to believe in individualism, they refused to help these individualists.

When the Progressive Conservative party came out with their national platform, promising farmers adequate parity prices and printed the words "adequate parity" in capital letters so that farmers would not miss the point, I believed they meant what they said. Being the only party that could defeat the government, I was hoping that they would win the election. The night of election day I was happier over the Conservative victory than I was over my own. When the new government took over and the strongest supporter of parity prices became the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), I was sure they would keep their word. When parliament opened on October 14 and it was stated in the speech from the throne that the government would introduce a measure to stabilize farm prices so that farmers would get a fair share of the national income, I believed it and so did the farmers. But when on October 31, the day the resolution was introduced in the house, I saw to my surprise that the word "fair" was missing from the resolution I began to wonder whether it was used in the throne speech only for the purpose of window dressing on Queen's day and then was to be forgotten.
My doubt increased to suspicion when discussion of that resolution was delayed, for no good reason, until December 11th, when on that grey December morning, the Minister of Agriculture explained the details of this proposed new farm price stabilization legislation. It struck me like a thunderbolt. I will never forget that moment when our new Minister of Agriculture revealed his detached, benevolent interest in the farmers' welfare in such an obviously disappointing form. That was the morning when I began to realize fully that the Conservative promise of parity prices was nothing more than a political smoke screen, and that the farmers once again, as so many times in the past, became the victims of cheap ambition and political chicanery.
It shocked me to the point where, when my time came to speak, I could not even take it seriously. I could not help but laugh at the minister's new invention to save the sinking farmers. In my ironical mood I went so far in my condemnation as to call it a joke. Today, Mr. Speaker, all I can say is that I am glad that after all the determined efforts of the minister to pooh-pooh our criticisms he finally did agree that it was a joke, withdrew his first bill and brought in a revised one.
After studying his amendments, however, I came to the conclusion that the best one is the nicely worded and high sounding preamble, and if the principle of maintaining

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
a fair relationship between prices and costs which is there referred to were implemented in the bill itself, then it would be of the highest standard. But that is not the case. Therefore I would suggest to the minister in all sincerity that the only difference between his first bill and the one we are now trying to refer to the committee is that the first one was a big joke and this one is a joke.
There is nothing in this reprinted bill which provides for establishment of support prices for farm products to bring about a fair relationship between the costs of goods and services which the farmer must buy in order to operate and	the prices	he	willreceive. It completely ignores the principle of parity, but that is what this government promised before and after election. I have here a report of a speech made by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) to the Saskatchewan farmers'	union	convention,	as	reported in the Winnipeg Free Press of December 6, 1957:
Hon. Alvin Hamilton, resources minister said Thursday night the federal government "has before it an agricultural stabilization bill to put agriculture on a relatively equal footing with other industries in Canada . . . The farmer needs support prices that enable him to meet his production costs . . .
That is what	he said	and I was	told	thatwhen he said it	he had	in his hand	the	first
bill. That is what I call cheap ambition.
Let us now analyse this improved bill which we are now asking should be submitted to the committee and see how far this is away from that promise. It consists of two parts. Firstly, guaranteed prices may be established as prescribed by the governor in council or the cabinet on agricultural commodities designated as such by the governor in council in terms of a percentage of the base price based on the average market price in the preceding 10 years. Secondly, there will be an annual adjusted mandatory minimum floor price of no less than 80 per cent of this base price for named commodities such as cattle, hogs, sheep, butter, cheese and eggs and wheat, oats and barley produced outside of the designated area as defined by the wheat board act.
For the operation of this scheme the bill provides for the establishment of a revolving fund of $250 million, the appointment of a board by the government to administer the act and an advisory committee appointed by the Minister of Agriculture to advise the minister and the board with respect to the stabilization of prices of agricultural commodities referred to it by the minister or the board. The governor in council may accept, alter or reject recommendations.
Outside of the additional $50 million which is added to the $200 million provided for under the old Agricultural Prices Support Act the first part of this new price support program is for all practical purposes identical to the one instituted by the Liberals.
The old as well as the new scheme does not provide for support prices to be set at a fair relationship to the cost in spite of the fact that this is what the government promised it would do if elected. As soon as it was elected this government forgot that it is only fair that we should look at the institution of farm support prices in the same way that we look at the existence of minimum wages. Minimum wages were established for the purpose of protecting labour from exploitation and guaranteeing them a minimum standard of living. Apparently the government does not know that farmers are simply asking for the same kind of minimum protection that other working people have enjoyed for years. How can the farmers sell their products for less than a parity price when parity, in reality, means no more than a price equal to cost of production.
Those who suggest that the Canadian primary producers should continue to sell for less than it cost them to produce-as they have been doing for years-are economic nitwits who have neither the ability to think nor the capacity to feel. Such kind of thinking borders on lunacy, because it cannot possibly be done without ruining the farmers and the country too.
Not only is this major principle omitted from this plan, but neither the board nor the committee have power to set prices; they can only advise the minister, and they can only do so on such matters and with regard to such problems as are referred to them by the minister. How many will be referred to them? The power of decision under this new plan as well as under the old as to what product shall be supported, and on what level will rest with the cabinet or, in the ultimate analysis, with the Minister of Agriculture in exactly the same way as under the existing Agricultural Prices Support Act. The parallel between the new bill and the old act can raise goose-flesh on anyone with a good memory. When farm prices went down, the former minister of agriculture was occupying himself with juggling figures, trying desperately to prove that the farmers were never better off and that they required no support under their prices. How worthless the old support program turned out to be under the direction of a political mind shrouded in confusion behind a skull which acted like an iron curtain can be seen by reading one paragraph
3426	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization from the last report issued by the prices support board of which I have a copy. I quote:
As indicated in the tabular summary below, the total net cost from the start of operations in 1946 to March 31, 1957, was $94,084,716.91. Of this total, about $70 million was attributable to the losses on the extensive buying and selling programs undertaken for hogs and cattle as an emergency measure following the embargo on the shipment of livestock and livestock products to the United States during the foot-and-mouth disease outbreak from February 25, 1952 to March 1953.
If you deduct the $70 million used as an emergency measure, as stated in the report- a sum which no doubt would have been available anyway without a prices support act-it becomes clear that only $24 million has been used in 11 years to support farm prices in spite of the fact that during the last six years prices have been falling more and more out of line with costs. Does the minister really think that after the unhappy experience farmers have had with this old price support scheme he can get away with blowing up another similar political bubble under which he has the power to appoint the personnel of the committee, the power to decide which products shall be referred to the committee for study and the power to make a final decision as to when and how supports shall be applied? How can he possibly believe that farmers will again accept anything in which the degree of application depends almost entirely on the caprice of one man?
It is not within the prerogative of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) to decide on what level unemployment insurance is to be paid; it is set out in the Unemployment Insurance Act what the amount shall be, and not left to the political mood of a few men or even of one man. In other words, it is guaranteed by the law. Why then, does this bill not set out what prices shall be paid for agricultural products? Why must the setting of farm prices come more or less within the prerogative of one man to decide instead of under the jurisdiction of the fair and just law of this land. This is the kind of protection other people have.
Can it be, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Agriculture is of the opinion that he will be as fair and as just as the law of the land, that he will have regard to the cost of production in setting these guaranteed prices and that farmers should therefore trust him? We trusted the former minister of agriculture, and what happened?

He did quite a good job
with you.
He juggled us around and he juggled us down until we landed in hell.
Tell us how you got your farms.
And then he stood beside it, throwing snowballs to lower the temperature -about $2 million a year he threw to us for 11 years.

Tell us about the socialist
system.
Try making a speech yourself.
If I made one I would try to make a contribution.
You could not do a job like this.
I am speaking frankly, perhaps more frankly than I ever did before.

You usually don't speak
frankly.
How are you going to vote on this matter?
Why are the socialists worrying about how anyone votes.

I repeat, I am speaking frankly, perhaps more frankly than I have ever done before. I have no good reason to believe that the economic horizon of our new minister is wider than that of the old one. If it were, he would have already used the present prices support act. The act is there, the money is there, the board is there-but he is not there. Watching his performance in the house on the discussions of declining farm prices I have reached the conclusion that his thinking on this point is more restricted than that of the former minister. His desperate attempt to deny the fact that farm prices are still declining provides conclusive proof of this contention. Take, for example, November 14 when, as reported on page 1106 of Hansard, he was asked what he would do to stop the constant decline in cattle prices. Here is his answer:
Now I do not know of the drastic drop in livestock prices to which my hon. friend and various other people who have made this statement in prefacing questions are referring.
At the same time he tried to prove that cattle prices went down only $2 in two years and stated that this cannot be regarded as a drastic drop.
They are up higher now than they have been for two years.
On what level are you going to support them?
The member for Springfield is running a sports shop; he would not know those things.
He does not read the papers.

The curious thing to me was this. He went back two years to prove that

the price o f good steers had not gone down but what he did not tell us was that between December 1956 and December 1957 the price of good steers declined from $20.97 to $17.86.
What is the price now for those good steers?
I am talking about the situation at that time.
Ask him the price of hockey sticks. He will know that.
Footballs would be better, they are full of wind.

On November 26, as recorded at page 1510 of Hansard the minister was again asked a question as to what he would do with regard to falling livestock prices to which he replied:
I would like to point out, however, as I have done before that this habit of prefacing a question with a statement about a drastic and continuing fall in prices is not one which is borne out by the latest statistics which I have received. As a matter of fact during the past week or ten days prices of both cattle and hogs have gone up from $1 to $1.50 per hundred. The price of lambs is up about $2 to $2.50 per hundred, and the general level of poultry prices and so forth is higher than it was at this time last year and higher than a few months ago.
The minister went back only one week or ten days to prove to us that prices were not going down. Just think of that. But he did not tell us that since he took office the price of good steers fell from $19.72 in July 1957 to $17.86 in September 1957. At the same time the price of hogs dropped from $37.75 in July 1957 to $30.50 in September 1957. The price of lambs fell from $24.57 in July 1957 to $22.33 in September 1957. And by the way, for the information of the house, I would point out that I took these figures from the very same pamphlet the minister used that morning to disprove that prices were going down. This is what I call real juggling. This is the reason I have lost confidence in the minister and in the bill and I can assure him I am not alone in this respect. The farmers have lost confidence too. In order to prove that point I will read a paragraph from a letter which I received from a farmer's wife in Ontario who writes:
The agricultural minister has no need to wonder why all questions pertaining to agriculture are prefaced with the observation about the drastic state of farmers, and the reduction in their income. You would think he had been living on a desert island for a long time, that he has to be told repeatedly of these things.
This is representative of what the farmers think of the minister. I do not think there has ever been a minister in history who lost the respect of the people he represents faster than did our present Minister of Agriculture with his bill.
Senate and House of Commons Act
This should make it clear that under the circumstances the first part, the enforcement of which depends on the minister cannot be depended upon and therefore is practically worthless. I would not dare ask farmers to accept it or to rely on it.
What about the second part of that bill? The second part is not only worthless but dangerous. Several key commodities which I have enumerated before would be supported by a permanent floor price at 80 per cent of the average market price of the preceding ten years. This low floor price-or should we call it basement price-would no doubt react unfavourably on the price structure and actually provide an incentive for the trade to push prices down to that low level. Why-should they pay more than the floor price if they do not have to? I have long suspected that low floor prices are more of a detriment than a benefit to farmers although I could not prove it. But now we have the admission of the former minister of agriculture which he made on December 20 as recorded at page 2673 of Hansard where he stated that by setting low support prices the government is giving an indication to the trade that this is the price the government thinks ought to be paid for the commodity and the tendency will be to gravitate towards that price.

the second reading of Bill No. 22, to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to proceed with this bill at this time. In introducing Bill No. 22, an act to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act, I believe I am putting into effect the wishes that have been expressed by many Canadians. I know that view has been expressed on many occasions by members of this house and it has been expressed on more than one occasion by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker); that is, to put into effect a means of taking the attendance in the House of Commons. The principle of taking attendance is one that is generally accepted in all walks of life and in all business endeavours and I see no reason why it should not be rightly accepted in the dispatch of government business.
The bill which I am moving is a simple one. It is Bill No. 22, entitled an act to amend the

Senate and House of Commons Act Senate and House of Commons Act and it involves an addition to subsection 1 of section 45 of the Senate and House of Commons Act in the following words:
Provided that the attendance shall be taken during each sitting day and a list of members present annexed to the Votes and Proceedings of the House of Commons of each day.
Section 45, as hon. members will realize, refers to the declaration which hon. members shall make at the conclusion of each month in order to collect their pay from the treasury office. In that case, as we know, it is required that members make a statutory declaration of the number of days' absence. But the bill goes one step further. The explanatory note reads as follows:
The purpose of this amendment is to acquaint the Canadian people with the attendance of their elected representatives in the parliament of Canada.
In the interests of democracy I believe the more information we can get across to the Canadian people the more efficient that democracy will be. The principle of taking attendance in legislative bodies is accepted in the other place, as hon. members will realize upon looking at the minutes of the proceedings of the Senate of Canada. They will find in each day's proceedings a list of the senators present during that day's activities. Therefore, I would hardly expect any members to complain about accepting this bill on the basis of reflecting on their reputation.
I want it understood at the start that the bill does not mean that members are required to remain in their seats in the House of Commons during all of the debates, and I am afraid that conception might be generally held. I think that would be rather unfair punishment to inflict on anyone. Hon. members should have the opportunity to go behind the curtain for a smoke or to attend to their other business. All the bill does is to provide that some means should be utilized to indicate when members are in attendance in the House of Commons and to provide an indication of which members are absent during the dispatch of government business.
I recall that when I was a university student I had no objection to the professor marking the vacant seats during the lecture each day. There was a purpose for that, to make certain that the hard-earned money of our parents was being spent to good advantage. Here we are being paid to attend to government business, to represent our constituents in the House of Commons, and I can see no reason why we should not have our attendance taken on the same basis.
In outlining a proposal which I think would be practicable I do not want to provoke an argument as to the various


techniques which could be used in taking the attendance. But all parties will agree with me that the most important part of the proceedings on any day is the opening period during orders of the day. It would seem to follow that that is the most important period of the day and it would not be asking too much of hon. members to be in their places for the first 15 minutes of orders of the day so that their presence could be noted by an official of the House of Commons. In the event that a member was occupied with other engagements and unable to be here he would simply need to state to the official that he was unable to be here at that time but was present in the building and he would be accepted as having been present. A list could then be placed in Votes and Proceedings for public perusal.
The business of running the country by means of a democratic parliament is of such importance that it means the constant attention of those who are selected by the people to present their views and ideas. I should point out that one of the accomplishments of the minority position of the government at the present time has been the maintenance of good attendance by members of parliament. In theory at any rate there is a constant threat of the government being defeated. At one time last evening I thought the threat was going to be even greater than it appears to be because a certain incident was going to be happening soon. However, we find that "soon" can mean several things. During the last parliament, however, the Liberal party had a great majority, a majority so large, in fact, that all the members west of the city of Ottawa could have stayed home and the government would have been sustained on a confidence vote, but this week, however, all the Liberals in Canada were in Ottawa which was the reverse of the other situation.
I think we can safely assume that members of the House of Commons will participate in voting if they are present in Ottawa. Let us look at the record of the previous parliament. The average attendance for votes called on a Monday in the years 1953, 1954 and 1955 is 143 members out of a total of 264 who could vote. On Tuesday there is some improvement, 174, with a further increase on Wednesday to 186. The peak voting attendance was on Thursday, with 189 members. On Friday during that same period the average declined to 132, which means that less than half the members of the House of Commons were expressing their views on the issues to be decided by means of the vote.
We find that on Mondays last year there was an average attendance of 144 for votes and on Tuesdays 149. On Wednesdays there

was an increase to 186. On Thursdays the attendance was 178, with the tragic figure of 102 members being represented in Friday votes. It is small wonder that many members of the House of Commons have been labelled "T to T boys", those who show up on Tuesday and leave on Thursday. As a member of the previous parliament I recall sitting beside my deskmate and our inquiring from each other who members across the way were because in the four years we had sat there we had not seen them often enough to place them. I presume they were some of the individuals who perhaps found their occupations calling them on Mondays and Fridays.
There is evidence that absenteeism still exists because on the very day that this bill was introduced, November 4, I made a personal count of the members of the Liberal party who were present and noted that only 43 out of a possible 106 were in their places during orders of the day. That, of course, was on a Monday. It is indeed to the credit of the government members that their attendance was so complete I was unable to count the number absent on that particular day.
This problem is not a new one. It is not one that has developed in recent years because Mr. J. Redlich, a professor at the University of Vienna, in his book, "The Procedure of the House of Commons", volume I, points out the following at page 43:
Repeated attempts were made to secure the attendance of members in the house by orders threatening fines for unauthorized absence.
He is referring to the British House of Commons. The footnote points out the following:
The expedient does not seem to have been very successful. At all events, the modern complaint that towards the end of the session the numbers in attendance diminished considerably goes back to Elizabethan times.
Further light is cast on the subject in volume II, page 105, of Mr. Redlich's book, where he says:
The party system has a very marked effect upon one prominent feature of parliamentary life-the attendance of members. The large number of the representatives of the people, and the considerations of space which have been described above, when taken together, make it almost a physical impossibility for all members to be present at the same time; as in other parliaments, there are great variations in the number who attend. The House of Commons being a politically sovereign assembly, this variation, unless guarded against, would involve great risks to a government which is absolutely dependent upon the constant support of a majority of those present.
The consequence is that there has never been a time when complaints of the absence of often quite a large proportion of the members have not been heard. The means adopted in earlier years for enforcing the duty of attendance, such as calls of the house (of which more in the historical note) have long been abandoned as futile. They have
Senate and House of Commons Act been replaced by other and more effective inducements. In the first place, there is a deepening of the feeling of responsibility of members to the electorate; this is itself a result of the gradual but decided increase in the dependence of representatives upon those who have sent them to parliament, which has followed the extension of the suffrage.
I think there is an indication, Mr. Speaker, of the history of absenteeism in the House of Commons. Mr. Redlich goes on to point out some of the techniques that were used to assure a full attendance in the house. The oldest method to ensure attendance was the roll call taken at a varying interval. The most ancient and the most severe penalty for a member not present when the roll was called was a direction to the sergeant-at-arms to arrest the deserter. The most ancient form of money penalty was the deprivation of salary.
Mr. Norman Ward in his book "The Canadian House of Commons" points out that the first and only serious attempt to tighten up the attendance regulations was made in 1920. At that time the maximum allowance for a member was raised to $4,000 for a session of more than 50 days, and a member was entitled to the full indemnity only if he attended three-quarters of the actual sittings of the house. Mr. Ward states:
The 1920 statute was revolutionary, and its effects most salutary.
A footnote quotes Mr. Fowler in the Senate debates of 1943 as saying:
Under the more stringent regulations now in force the attendance has been excellent.
Mr. Ward goes on to analyse the situation, and states:
So poor was the attendance among Conservative members during the long session of 1947-48, for instance, that several groups supporting the party outside of parliament proposed at a party convention to condemn absenteeism in the legislature.
The necessity of maintaining attendance in the house was not overlooked in drafting the standing orders of the House of Commons. Standing Order No. 5 states:
Every member is bound to attend the service of the house, unless leave of absence has been given him by the house.
The lax attendance which has been experienced has not gone unrecognized. In a news story in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of March 20, 1954, entitled "Howe Appeals for Higher Attendance", it is stated:
Acting Prime Minister C. D. Howe, at the Liberal M.P.'s caucus on Wednesday made a direct, earnest appeal to government supporters to improve their attendance while the House of Commons is in session.	[DOT]
Mr. Howe pointed out that the public will be watching members' attendance in the commons more closely in the future in the light of parliament's
3430	HOUSE OF
Senate and House of Commons Act action in increasing the $4,000 sessional indemnity to $8,000 per annum as from the commencement of the current session on November 12 last.
The commons has no attendance register and thus the vote on recorded divisions constitutes the only public indication of M.P.'s attendance.
We find also that in the Financial Times attention is being drawn to absenteeism. In an editorial dated March 23, 1956, we find this:
Perusal of Hansard during the last session, and to date in this session, indicates that absenteeism still is rife among M.P.'s. The week-enders are still at their old tricks; and it is even suggested that the weekends are stretching out.
The conclusion re-enforces the purpose of this bill and states that there are still remaining too many loopholes in the House of Commons' rules in the matter of attendance which can be taken advantage of by members who are slack in the exercise of their duties. They state that it behooves the elector to keep check on his representative and see that he does the job he is now being well paid for doing.
This session has not escaped the eyes of the press. The Ottawa Journal of November 12, 1957 states:
"Weekenditis" has returned to the House of Commons.
The article continues:
When the session began in the no-majority house almost every member was in his place every day.
Now the members from the west and the mari-times begin to growl that the long weekend means Monday absentees among their colleagues from the central provinces who can go home for the weekend conveniently.
It is obvious that consideration will have to be given to this important problem for the sake of the government. The privileges which we have gained as members of a democracy are historical and I think they should be safeguarded by whatever rules are necessary for their active enforcement. We know, as I have mentioned, that attendance is taken in the other place and is listed in the daily Votes and Proceedings, so the mechanics of doing so are far from impossible.
I do not think it is necessary to go into all the mechanics of fulfilling the spirit of this bill at this time. The mechanics could be worked out by a committee working in co-operation with the staff of the House of Commons. Any procedure that would be adopted would be offensive to those who, from time to time, are absent themselves. I do not expect any criticism will come from those who have been most diligent in their attendance. I am hoping for speedy passage of this measure because the Canadian people will benefit from it through more diligent and thus more complete representation.
[Mr. Johnson (Kindersley) .3

Mr. Speaker, we have before us now a rather interesting bill dealing with the subject of recording attendance at the sessions of the House of Commons. The hon. member who introduced the bill has given some historical account of the attendance in the House of Commons, and has pointed out that right from early days, back in Elizabethan times, there was some difficulty in having members attend as regularly as some people thought they should He traced the comments with regard to attendance right down to the present day. Obviously this is not a matter that has suddenly come to our attention or something which is new to this particular day and generation.
In the course of his remarks he pointed out that a record of a sort is maintained by the fact that members have to furnish the Clerk of the house with a statement indicating the number of days they have attended sessions during the month. In furnishing this statement a member may indicate the reason for his absence, whether it was due to illness or some unavoidable cause. It is quite obvious that if attendance is recorded, allowance has to be made, for instance, for illness or unavoidable absence. The hon. member who proposed the bill did not indicate just how that was going to be done. He is suggesting that every day, when Votes and Proceedings are printed, a list of the members who have been in attendance should be recorded therein. I presume that those who are unavoidably away or who are away by reason of illness, at some subsequent date would have to indicate that the fact they were not recorded was due to circumstances beyond their control. The subject becomes rather complicated when you begin to think of the various methods by which attendance might be recorded, and how you are going to make allowance for those who cannot be here.
The hon. member suggests that if the names; are recorded like this from day to day the public would then be fully informed. In political warfare I presume this would be extremely useful ammunition, enabling someone to recite that such and such a member had been absent on so many days during the course of the preceding session. To do that, of course, in the absence of the hon. member who had been away and not give him a chance to make his explanation would prove embarrassing. The difficulty sometimes with political life is that information of this nature might be used a little bit unfairly.
However, I was wondering what was in the mind of the hon. member in suggesting this procedure and what real purpose would

be served by this daily recording of attendance. He suggested that if this attendance record were taken in what he called the most important part of the daily proceedings which is before the orders of the day that would be a satisfactory time to make the record. I am no so sure that that is the most important part of the day's proceedings. It happens to be the period when members are here in the house in large numbers, when announcements are made from the government side and when questions are asked by hon. members. There may be a fair bit of interest in that particular part of the day which, during the course of this session, has stretched out to about an hour and a half. In other years it used to be limited to about 45 minutes. As I say, there may be a fair bit of interest in that particular part of the day but I am not so sure that that is the most important part of the day's proceedings. There is interest in seeing what type of question is asked and what type of answer is received, and frequently in my opinion not much is accomplished. I think that during the course of the actual debates in the house which come after the orders of the day are called much more important proceedings are carried out. However, the hon. member suggests that that is the time for the roll to be called and the members' attendance to be recorded.
Then he does not insist that the members should stay in the chamber. They may then go about their other duties. Of course there are other duties in the House of Commons. Frequently many committees are sitting here and members are obliged to leave and attend those committees. One committee is sitting this afternoon. I know that in other years we have counted the number of members engaged in committee work outside of the chamber, and that number has run to well over 100. Yet on those occasions someone has spied out the chamber and said, "'There are only 40 members present; what are they doing?", not giving them credit at all for the other work that is carried on by members of parliament.

speechtext:
Simply recording the attendance of members during the first hour of the day would not solve that particular problem at all. If the complaint is that members are not in the chamber and are not attending to their duties, this procedure will not keep them in the chamber. If the purpose is to ensure that they are in Ottawa each day of
Senate and House of Commons Act the week, it depends on where they live. They might record their attendance at, say, eleven o'clock in the morning, then disappear by car or by plane, return the following morning and again record their attendance. I see no purpose in that type of mechanical recording of attendance.
The hon. member who introduced this bill talked about democracy which to me has meant freedom of the individual. Yet he is suggesting certain restraints on individual freedom. Why should it be necessary to have a daily recording of the attendance of members during the first hour each day? Under our democratic system I think there is available to the people of this country a salutary check by means of which to deal with their members. We are obliged to face elections from time to time. At election period the people can decide whether or not their member is giving the service they expect to be given by a member of the House of Commons. They can take note of his activities during the session. They can hear reports from time to time. Prior to a general election there is always a nominating convention at which delinquent members can be dealt with; and if they are not dealt with on that occasion, they can be dealt with when the votes are cast on election day. I think there is available to the general public, with regard to the members they send to Ottawa, the opportunity to determine whether or not they are adequately represented, without having a daily check list showing whether or not members were in Ottawa at say eleven o'clock from Monday to Friday or, as we have it now, from Monday to Saturday.
This matter is tied up with attendance within the chamber. When matters of vital importance are under consideration the chamber, in my experience, has been very well filled. When matters of less importance are under consideration, the chamber has not been so well filled, not because the members who are absent from the chamber are not aware of what is going on but because, being aware of the subject that is under discussion and knowing that some of their colleagues will be present to look after things, but because they feel that their presence is not at that moment required.
If this bill were passed and this rigidity imposed upon members of parliament I think it would be an unnecessary imposition on them. We have had this subject brought forward previously under other circumstances. I have weighed the issue in my own mind over several years and I fail to see any value that would result from the proposition put before us. I think this is no way in which to measure the service of elected members of
3432	HOUSE OF
Senate and House of Commons Act parliament. The position that is accorded us here is given to us by the free votes of the people. They send their representatives to the House of Commons to represent them, put forward their case and conduct the business of the country. From time to time they change their representatives at Ottawa. Over the years this method has worked and has been found to be satisfactory. The people who complain about the non-attendance of members are seldom the ones who are in this chamber themselves or who are steady attendants of this chamber.
The people who complain are frequently those who have no particular responsibility in parliament but who are observers of the scene and are perhaps not aware of the duties performed by members of the House of Commons.

The duties of a member of the House of Commons, irrespective of the side of the house on which he sits, are heavy. I have been here long enough to appreciate that and I know that representing a constituency takes many hours of a member's time in dealing with correspondence and in dealing with visitors or delegations of interested bodies who have suggestions to make with regard to legislation. I do not know of any member of the House of Commons who has not, during the course of his experience here, found that it is an onerous duty to deal with all the matters I have


mentioned and, at the same time, to keep himself informed on matters of public interest and all the things which are coming before the house from day to day requiring his attention either by way of debate or decision when he is called upon to vote, or in the work of the various committees which meet from time to time.
I have never found that there has been much spare time available for a member of the House of Commons if he is anxious to enlarge his knowledge of public affairs and I think this is the experience of many new members who are in this present parliament. These members are seeing things from the inside now and they are I am sure, discovering that there is an immense amount of material to be studied if they want to be informed on all the subjects which come before this house. About 20 departments are represented by the government and each department has subdivisions. Each department has an immense amount of literature published with regard to it or on its behalf and for a member of the House of Commons to inform himself adequately with regard to subjects considered by the house he has to put in a great deal of time on such work. That prevents him from always being in the chamber and, on occasion, even prevents him from being in Ottawa.
The hon. member who introduced this bill made no provision for the legitimate requests of constituents for their member to visit them and to speak at meetings in his home constituency or in other places. It is one of the duties of members of parliament to carry the message to the people of Canada by travelling to and fro across this country and by speaking at meetings.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT

I am not, of course, suggesting that too much time should be spent in that way but we should make allowances for it. The hon. member with his suggested attendance record would not make any allowance whatsoever for that and how could it be explained?

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ATTENDANCE OF MEMBERS

Nevertheless the hon. member's attendance record is a daily attendance record despite the 21 days allowed under the act and, for these absences, what provision will he make with regard to explanation? How is that explanation to be made? It is much too complicated.
In my opinion, in suggesting rigid systems such as this, the hon. member is attempting to lower the position of a member of the House of Commons. There may be occupations in which rigid attendance records should be kept, but surely this is not one of them. He made reference to university days-

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ATTENDANCE OF MEMBERS
speechtext: And the Senate.

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ATTENDANCE OF MEMBERS
speechtext:
-when records were kept of a person's attendance. In my days at university, I would inform the hon. member, no records were kept of our attendance. We were considered to be responsible people. Most of us were not spending our parents' hard-earned money, we were spending money which we had earned ourselves and no record was kept. We had to stand or fall on what we gained from our opportunities at university. Once you impose the rigidity of daily attendance you take something away from that person and you do not put him on his own. Looking back at my university days I would say ours was a better system than that in which records must be kept from day to day. It placed the responsibility exactly where it belonged and I think the same is true with respect to members of parliament. They stand or fall on their own record.
Hon. members make their own contribution here in the House of Commons and elsewhere throughout the country, and the people decide whether or not they are
Senate and House of Commons Act adequate representatives. There are members of the House of Commons who may come here about six times in the course of a session and who yet make a more effective contribution to the proceedings of this house than, perhaps, do others who may be here on many more occasions.

It is not pay for daily attendance here.
The hon. member has, I am sure, certain ideas of regimentation in his mind which, I think, are not applicable to the type of work which is performed by the House of Commons, and for these reasons and others which I could enumerate, but prefer not to discuss because I wish to allow other hon. members an opportunity to speak, I am inclined to vote against this bill.

We have been elected by the votes of the people, and the situation is surely different. I have been submitted in my lifetime to as much regimentation as anyone in this chamber, and I resist this type of regimentation. I have worked in institutions where we were forced to sign a book when we came in, and I have refused to sign because I do not like that way of doing business, yet nobody fired me. I would never ask employees working under me to sign a book saying whether they came in at nine o'clock or 9.05 or even 9.25. I do not like that kind of regimentation. A man stands or falls on his ability and on his contribution to the job.

Senate and House of Commons Act

maintopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ATTENDANCE OF MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say at the outset that I personally am not in favour of Bill No. 22. I should like to endorse the argument which has been advanced by the hon. member who has just spoken. To put the matter very plainly, I do not think members of parliament should be treated like school children.
I should like to say further that I do not believe the employees who work in this building should be obliged to punch time clocks, because I think they have a demoralizing influence. To some extent at least they require a man to be here at a certain time, and I think it would be much better to respect our employees more and do away with time clocks. I think this bill is an example of regimentation, and in any event the particular proviso requiring that attendance should be taken during each sitting day is poorly constructed. While I do not agree with the proviso, I would point out that it does not make clear the time when the attendance should be taken. You might have a situation where a member arrives at 11 o'clock in the morning and leaves, say, after the question period, and does not return to the House of Commons that day. On the other hand, if there were a definite hour inserted as to the time of the roll call, a member could turn up at that time, sit for a short while and then leave.
The present system is an honour system and the responsibility is placed squarely on the shoulders of the member of parliament himself and if the people he represents feel he is not measuring up to what is expected of him in the House of Commons, then under our democratic system of government they have a remedy and they have a right to elect somebody else to represent them.
I do not think that attendance in the House of Commons is necessarily an indication of the work which a member does for his country. Members of parliament could be here from the opening of the parliamentary day at, say 11 in the morning to 10 o'clock at night, except for the usual intermissions, and yet those same members could be guilty of neglecting their constituents by not paying proper attention to their problems. I feel that the average member of parliament irrespective of party often spends long hours at his work. I know myself of members who leave this building sometimes at two or three o'clock in the morning and who work seven days a week. If attendance is taken and if a certain amount of regimentation is introduced it might influence such members to say "What's the use?" and render less service to their country than they are doing at the present time.

I do not see any real purpose in this bill. I favour the honour system which is now in existence, and I submit that the present system is producing the best results for the country.
