Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who has put this resolution forward is a very close personal friend of mine, and I know that in advancing this proposal he has done so with the most sincere intent.
He is from western Canada, and because of the great expanse of geography in this country hon. members who come from more remote parts of the country are, perhaps, in attendance more frequently than are those whose constituencies lie closer at hand. I further know that the hon. member has a very laudable purpose in bringing this legislation forward; he is desirous that the best quality of service be given in the performance of public duties by all hon. members of this house. However, I am forced to agree with the two previous speakers that he is trying to do the right thing in the wrong way. I mean by that that he is trying to improve the quality of representation in the house by legislative compulsion.
I do not think I need to re-echo the sentiments of those who have spoken earlier in this debate. In a democracy where individual responsibility is of the essence, it would not be desirable to endeavour to improve the quality of representation by compulsory means. We are, of course, guided here according to the tradition established in the mother of parliament at Westminster, and in that chamber, as I recall, having visited it particularly during the war years, there is not even a separate seat for every member. The voluntary system, the system of placing the responsibility on the shoulders of the individual members of parliament, is carried out to the maximum extent there. It is understood, under the type of parliamentary system that operates both in the United Kingdom and in this country the areas of responsibility are so great that it is unreasonable to expect a member of parliament to spend all of his time in the legislative chamber.
I could spend some time this afternoon outlining the multiplicity of tasks that fall to the lots of members of parliament. Certainly quite basic is our responsibility to attend the debates of the House of Commons in the chamber itself but outside of that, as has been so eloquently pointed out by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill), we have responsibilities in the constituency, in committee work and revolving around our work in the office which

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.

speechtext:
The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Harkness for the second reading of Bill No. 237, to provide for the
3436	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization stabilization of the prices of agricultural commodities, and the amendment thereto of Mr. McCullough.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in continuing from where I left off this afternoon I want to say that choosing the last 10 years as the period for calculating the base price and then making it a moving period is another factor that will facilitate a downward price movement. In the first place, the price of farm products in that period was completely out of line with the cost and therefore it should never have been chosen. It does not make sense. As the period moves on, the spread between price and cost will widen from year to year. This downward price trend will affect the calculation of the base price to a greater degree year after year. As the high price years are progressively removed from the gradually falling 10-year moving average, the guaranteed minimum level will fall correspondingly. Within four years, when the high-price years of 1948, 1949, 1950 and 1951 are removed, the base price will be calculated on the average market price of 10 low-price years.
As a matter of fact, the present low market prices, which average about 80 per cent of parity, will actually become the base price and the mandatory floor price will be set at 80 per cent of that lower and lower sinking base price. It will bring the minimum floor price to the low level of about 64 per cent of parity or, in other words, 46 per cent below the cost of production.
Here is an example of what will happen. The price of butter on the Toronto market for 1957 was 60.6 cents per pound which should bring the 80 per cent permanent floor price for the year to 49.6 cents. If the market price for the next four years should average the same as in the last four years, the minimum guarantee for 1962 would decline to 48.4 cents, a drop of 12.2 cents a pound.
The price of cheese in 1957 was 34.1 cents per pound. The 80 per cent permanent floor price would be 27 cents and for 1962 it would fall to 25.9 cents, a drop of 8.2 cents. The egg price for 1957 was 51.6 cents. The minimum guarantee would be 45.4 cents and by 1962 it would go down to 44.6 cents, a drop of 7.2 cents a dozen.
When one analyses the text of the bill from every angle and figures out its meaning he can hardly believe that a government could bring forward such an absurd proposal. Only confused mortals with a worm's eye view, harbouring dark and unholy thoughts, could think of such an idea. When you think that farm prices in the last few years have proven
[Mr. Rynard.l

to be more out of line with costs than at any time in history but are used as a measuring stick to set floor prices, it is even too ridiculous for further comment.
In what court of justice could this bill stand up without being condemned as the greatest betrayal in our history when compared with the need and the promise? No wonder the minister is refusing to refer it to the committee. He knows that it would never stand the scrutiny of ordered minds. He should know that the whole thing has no principle, no heart and no soul. He must know that it is nothing more than a bundle of contradictory platitudes.
What other reason could he have for refusing to turn it over to a committee established by parliament for the purpose of studying such matters concerning agriculture? When he was asked to do so he claimed it would take too much time. But that was on the eleventh of December. Today is the seventeenth of January. So even this alibi does not stand up when put under the spotlight of existing facts.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the representative of a mostly agricultural constituency, it is my duty, I think, to say a few words in this house about this bill.
The agricultural class of my constituency has been making, and is still making, almost heroic efforts to live modestly out of the land. I do not exaggerate when I say that 80 per cent of our farmers are not satisfied with their lot and I do say this, all the more convinced that I am by the fact that, due to my former duties, I have visited these good people three or four times a year in the last twenty years of my life.
It is illogical, Mr. Speaker, that our farmers, who are almost the sole factor of our survival as Canadians, should be abandoned to the whims and requirements of business, and be made the victims of the progress of modern industry.
The present agricultural crisis is the result, I think, of three main causes.
(1)	The industrial development of this country, which is fast changing the old economic and social pattern, has put the farmers at a disadvantage with regard to the other classes of our society, as they are unable to get together and protect themselves adequately against their well-organized enemies who exploit them at every turn.

(2)	The necessity to mechanize their farms at high cost while having to sell their produce at a ridiculous and disproportionate price.
(3)	The natural dislike of young people for farming, where they have to put in much effort and sacrifice to earn a living for their family; while, on the other hand industry seems to offer them a far greater security at a lesser effort, as well as comfort and leisure.
Because of these three reasons, I commend the government and I am pleased that a bill has been put before us which should considerably improve the farmer's lot.
The three parties forming the opposition are voicing bitter criticisms and seem to me very anxious about the possible results of this legislation. They have a perfect right to do so-for my part, I want to be more confident. I can't seem to convince myself that the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) is asking us to approve this bill in order to lower farm prices. I believe he really wants to improve conditions, and I hope he will succeed.
I would have liked to see parity prices, as the hon. members of the Liberal, C.C.F. and Social Credit parties are asking, but it seems that such an experiment, which has been made abroad is a very costly one, and that it would be a very onerous mistake for our country to pass such legislation.
I would not have objected to a mistake on the part of the government benefiting the farmers of this country, for governments have rarely made mistakes which were profitable to agriculture.
Since I have had the honour of sitting in this house, I find that hon. members opposite have many more chances than government members to make known, on the floor of this house, the needs of their ridings or of their provinces. It is probably for that reason that the farm difficulties in the province of Quebec have not always been pointed out here, I think, as they should have been. When I see my hon. friends from the western provinces urge so forcefully a subsidy on their grains, I realize the trend of events does not run a smooth course in their area. The province of Quebec, through its members, has sometimes given the impression that conditions were not so bad among our farmers.
Mr. Speaker, may I point out that 80 per cent of the farmers in my riding live from hand to mouth, and are finding it very hard to make ends meet.
By poorly I do not mean that they are ill-fed or ill-clad. I mean that in order to remain
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization on their farm the whole family must take a hand in the work of the farm. The mother, the sons and daughters help to do various jobs according to their ability. To earn a gross annual income of $5,000, as most workers in the various trades earn fairly readily nowadays, a farmer requires 125 acres of good land and 15 good milch cows; he must sell $1,500 worth of hogs, calves and eggs each year, and to do this, the whole family has to help out.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, you can see that, from the point of view of personal income, the comparison is a sorry one between farmers and other classes of society. Oh, I know that the farmer enjoys some family and social advantages which cannot be expressed in terms of dollars. Those advantages are very important and the farmer himself tends to forget them, impressed as he is by the false and misleading appearances of the so-called comforts enjoyed by other classes of society. And it is precisely because of this natural tendency for our young farmers to look to those places where it seems to them life is easier that the government must spare no effort, no sacrifice, to make agriculture a paying proposition.
For any number of reasons which I have no time to set out here, the farmer has been left to himself without protection, whereas the other classes of society, from the representatives of government to lumber workers, have organized for the solution of those problems peculiar to their business or avocation.
Meanwhile, however, especially during the past ten years, the farmers as a class have been helplessly caught in the fluctuations of trade and industry. While industry grows rich at their expense, the consumers are paying through the nose for what the farmers, after working extremely hard, are selling at a ridiculously low price.
I will go a step further and say that the survival of our agricultural community and perhaps even the survival of Canada itself depends on the stabilization of the prices paid to our farmers at the same level or in proportion with other manufactured products.
You may believe that I exaggerate but I am convinced that we cannot go on forever asking the same people to make all the sacrifices while in so many other trades salaries are getting higher and higher for increasingly shorter hours of work.
Mr. Speaker, I have confidence in the agricultural bill introduced by the hon. Minister of Agriculture because the bill provides that a commission made up of representatives of the farmers shall set prices according to the cost of production.

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
One must have lived 25 years among farmers to know how often they have been threatened with insecurity and at the price of what efforts and sacrifices they have managed to survive. It is through their willingness to work and their sense of responsibility that they have managed to surmount so many difficulties.
Is it normal, Mr. Speaker, that a product like milk, when sold by farmers around cities, for daily consumption, should bring more than twice the price normally paid for milk going into the production of butter? It means that the farmer living close to a city sells his milk to the dairies at $4.65 to $4.75 a hundred pounds, while the farmer selling the same milk to butter factories gets only from $2.00 to $2.25 a hundred pounds. How many times have I seen farmers selling their eggs 30 cents to 35 cents a dozen when their cost of production was from 40 cents to 45 cents, or sell their hogs, their potatoes and other agricultural products below cost!
The rural community of my riding and it is also the case of most ridings in the province of Quebec, has not benefited as much as the other sections of the population from the necessary protection on the part of governments.
Mr. Speaker, this bill must by all means put an end to such disorder and social discrimination. The survival of the country depends on our farm population, and it is time and only fair that the country should sacrifice the millions required to keep the farmer attached to the land he still owns.
If the bill of the hon. Minister of Agriculture does, as I believe it will, reach its goal, farmers will sell their milk, butter, cheese, hogs, maple syrup, potatoes, beef, wheat, and poultry at prices from 15 to 20 per cent higher. For such a higher price, the consumer will ask for a better product, and the producer will be more interested in improving the quality of his produce.
I recognize that the technicians of the commission will be faced with difficulties, but the government managed to solve much more difficult problems than that. During my last campaign, I pledged myself to fight to my last breath on behalf of the farm people who so heroically fought for survival, and I am convinced that without their acceptance of continual privations and their typical spirit of sacrifice, the disaster would be much greater still.
As a proof that things are going wrong, the provincial agricultural credit has had to finance almost 60 per cent of the farms in my riding. I am taking the percentage of my riding, but I could use the same percentage for perhaps the whole province.

Mr. Speaker, I feel it is my duty to ask the minister to put on the list of those products whose price is to be supported, the pulpwood cut by the farmer, that is to say that wood which the farmer grows on his own lot.
In my constituency, as in about every constituency in the province of Quebec, 60 per cent of the farmers cut from 20 to 25 cords of wood every winter to gain a little of that extra revenue which they cannot find in agriculture.
If, for instance, the farmer's pulpwood could, after grading according to needs, be sold $16 a cord in the case of poplar, $18 a cord in the case of fir, $22 a cord in the case of spruce, I am told that the companies would not hesitate to pay such a price for the graded product.
This grading would protect our forests, which would then be worked intelligently, and the bill moved by the minister would achieve a double purpose, namely, safeguard one of our greatest national resources and provide greater security and comfort for our farmers.
In spite of the difficulties which may arise from this bill, I believe that the benefits which the agricultural class will derive from it will be worth much more than the funds which its implementation will require.
It is urgent that energetic and positive steps be taken to help out our farmers, for this country absolutely cannot do without them.
I do hope, Mr. Speaker, that bill 237 now before us, notwithstanding a few disturbing points, will considerably improve the economic and social standard of our deserving agricultural population.

Mr. Speaker, many of the debates on agricultural matters in this house have been concerned mainly with the plight of this industry in

the prairie provinces. The problem of marketing our large surplus of wheat at a price adequate to maintain the industry has been one of our major concerns. Measures which we believe would assist the farmer until such markets are found has given rise to extended discussion and debate in the house. Then we have had questions arising from the operations of the wheat board, the allocation of box cars, the duties of the transport controller or whether or not such an officer is necessary as well as a host of other problems in that connection which have been dealt with. But now we have before us an agricultural measure which is much different from any of those which I have mentioned. It is one which proposes to by-pass that tremendously important phase of the agricultural economy and to stabilize the agricultural industry without reference to one of its most important commodities, namely wheat except that grown outside the area designated by the Canadian Wheat Board Act.
I know it may be argued that this is but one of several or many measures which together will be designed to bring stability to the agricultural industry. But if so I think it has been clearly indicated in the debates thus far that it is one which will apparently contribute very little to the achievement of that objective. We listened to a debate several days ago in which one of the government supporters spoke against a measure that was introduced by an opposition member because it was not comprehensive enough. He pointed out the weaknesses in it and the failures. But certainly, as we look at this particular measure tonight, we do not see where it will contribute very much to the stabilization of the agricultural economy across the country.
It is an act to provide for the stabilization of the prices of agricultural commodities. Mr. Speaker, I do not think anyone would take the position that the need for such action is unnecessary. It has been pointed out time after time in the house that agriculture was and is at the present time in a very serious position and that those who are engaged in that industry are waging a losing battle against great odds, namely increasing costs on the one hand and reduced prices on the other.
I should like to refer to an editorial from my own home town paper, the Abbotsford, Sumas and Matsqui News. I am sure that we all recognize the fact that this is a worthwhile paper, and an extremely important one in British Columbia. Under the heading of "1958 Prospects" we read the following:
In the Fraser Valley, our principal Industry Is agriculture and it faces an uncertain year in consequence of the general economic slowdown. Costs
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization have risen, and in some cases are still rising, for both dairymen and poultrymen. Yet another round of increases is likely early in the year if present indications are a reliable guide. Such a cost squeeze is hard on the most efficient farmer, and may prove disastrous for marginal operators.
Whether there will be increases in the price of farm products sufficient to compensate for the inflationary pressures which farmers are feeling is highly speculative. As a general rule, increases for the farmer do not come with sufficient speed to protect him from such cost squeezes.
I would suggest that this is indicative of conditions not only in my own area but right across the country. A little further on in the editorial we find this:
Basic outlook of Fraser valley agriculture is bright, because of its access to a growing metropolitan market. High cost factors, however, create problems which are accentuated in the Fraser valley and which call for understanding and assistance.
Mr. Speaker, the fact has been stressed here on many occasions that the farming population of Canada are receiving much less than their share of the national income. I do not think it is necessary to put further figures on record because they have already been placed on record a number of times not only in this debate but in others. But it would seem to me that there is a general recognition of the fact that our farming population are not receiving their fair share of the national income. In the speech from the throne that was given recently we read the following words:
In order to assure to the farmers of Canada a fair share of the national income, you will be asked to enact a measure to provide greater stability in the prices of their products. Every possible effort is now being made, and will continue to be made to seek new markets for agricultural products as well as to regain those that have been lost.
I should like to suggest that this is recognition on the part of this government that farmers have not been in the position where they have received their fair share of the national income. We have a promise that at least something definite was contemplated to remedy that injustice.
We have had farmers and farm representatives speak here in this house with respect to the requests that have been made by the farmers and by their organizations. Not only have they made the requests, but they have outlined clearly and positively the steps they felt were necessary in order to bring about what they considered was a proper recognition of their needs and a proper position of agriculture in the Canadian economy. They want a fair share of the national income. In order to achieve that objective they have requested parity prices for their products. They are desirous of having a measure of security which is at least in some respects comparable to that which is enjoyed by other categories

The agricultural price support act introduced by the Conservative government seems to be completely useless.
In the past support prices were set by a government board advised by a committee from farm organizations. Under the new act the system is the same.
The only real difference is that the new act gives a definite guarantee of a minimum price-but it is a worthless guarantee. It promises only that farm products covered under the act will not sell for less than 80 per cent of the average price for the preceding 10 years. Quite plainly that offers no hindrance to steadily falling prices.
Of course the government contends that it will actually set prices higher than the guaranteed price, keeping them in line with conditions in other sectors of the economy. That leaves the farmers subject to the whims of politicians and civil servants, just as they were before. They have tried that system and it isn't any good.
What they want, and what the Conservatives promised them, is parity.
The Minister of Agriculture now says no one is sure what parity is, but he thinks his new bill is pretty close to it. Conservatives seemed to know before the election, but in case they have forgotten, parity means a price that will return to the reasonably efficient farmer his cost of production plus a reasonable profit. It is a price that will go up when costs of machinery, feed, fertilizer, freight, wages, buildings, clothing and other things a farmer must pay for go up, and if they ever come down, it will come down too.
I will just go a little further down in the editorial.

Isn't it worth a few surpluses to make that many people ride the country's economic escalator instead of getting ground up in it?

In other words, you are narrowed down and restricted because of the fact that certain things have been written into the measure as it presently stands.
Some hon. members in the C.C.F. and Social Credit groups have suggested that when you draft a measure in rather general terms and leave it to the government to administer the act in a manner which will be helpful you are, by so doing, leaving the measure to the consideration of some one individual or some very few individuals. You are, as a matter 96698-218
of fact, making the whole government responsible under both the terms of this bill and the terms of the existing act for what is being done with the taxpayers' money. That is generally thought to be a reasonable thing to do, that is not to simply place money in the hands of the government to be expended and place the responsibility for the expenditure of it with some one else but to hold the government itself responsible for the expenditure of that money. Both of these measures do that.
Each time you write into a bill a section which says, "You must do it this way or that way; you cannot do it this way or you cannot do it that way," then you simply tie the hands of those who are trying to do a job in the interests of the people being served and for this reason I do not follow along or agree with that argument. The measure is in general terms similar to the terms of the existing act and I still maintain the position I took a month ago to the effect that this bill is not as flexible as the act is. In other words, you are tied down, for example, to taking a ten-year period in order to arrive at certain results. Under the act presently on the statute books this government could take a ten-year period, a five-year period or a three-year period. It is not bound to take any particular period and I would like to submit that it is not reasonable to think that you can take the same period and apply it to every one of the products that might be under consideration from time to time, the reason being that those things which influence the prices of different commodities are not the same in all cases over a period of ten, five or even three years. Many things happen in connection with crops that alter and affect the situation and therefore to limit the measure in this way would bind the government to the consideration of only certain commodities. The amendments have had the effect of making this measure less flexible.
As has been said by hon. members of the government and others, there is a great difference between the bill as it was originally brought down and the one that is before us now. I have the one which is before all members of the house at this time and the only outstanding difference between it and the first bill is the number of years that are specified. It was three years in the previous bill and it is ten years in the present one.
In addition to that some one has said there is a preamble to this bill and he rather liked the preamble to this bill as compared with the other bill which had no preamble at all. In the preamble of the bill now before us the government has enunciated what was contained in subclause 2 of clause 9 of the
3444	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization original act. The idea expressed in the preamble is carried on throughout the measure in order to state the same thing over and over again but there is no great difference between the two.
Some comments have been made about the operation of the existing act over the years. A statement which is made often was repeated by the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Schulz) this afternoon. He has been making it for a long time. He has been corrected many times but he still makes it. Of course, no one can stop him doing that and he goes right on saying it. His statement is to the effect that there was only $200 million provided under the old measure and there will be $250 million under this one, which he does not distinguish as being very different provided certain things happen. But he goes on from there to use figures to prove that only $26 million was utilized over the years under the old legislation.
Of course, that leaves out entirely the fact that the fund is a revolving fund under both measures. It is not an amount which is set up, which you are told you can spend and then when it is gone you get another $200 million and spend that. The fund is used in such a way as to set up a support price under a product and then the product is taken in at that particular price and it costs the government so much. Then it is disposed of and there may be no loss at all. As a matter of fact, in some cases there may be some profit.
But the revolving fund is there in order to make it possible to utilize the money for the purpose of supporting prices, although now it is called stabilizing prices. There is some argument whether there is any difference in the meaning of the terms. I think "support" is a better term to use than "stabilize". Nevertheless, the amount of money is there to be utilized for the one or the other purpose or for both purposes. When the board pays money out to buy and then sells the product it comes back in again and the better the administration of the act is and the better the handling of the whole proposition is the less will be the amount of money that will be spent and not be available to be used again by the board.
As a matter of fact, I would think if you had a board that got rid of $250 million every year with nothing coming back in you would be doing in an even more definite manner what we object to in connection with what has been done on the other side of the line. But under the measure we did have out over the whole period somewhere in the neighbourhood of $400 million, not $26 million, not $200 million. I can quite understand people saying that even that is not a great amount


when you consider that the legislation has been in existence over a considerable number of years. It has actually been in operation for about 11 years. It can be said that that is not a large amount of money to utilize and it would not be if you were handling grain and all the other commodities, but nevertheless there has been about $400 million used and I think at one particular time there was about $125 million out at one time.
It is suggested that $72 million of the amount was money that was put out in connection with the foot-and-mouth disease. It was intended when the legislation was drafted that any emergencies which arose that made it necessary to support prices to the farmer could be dealt with under the act. It was broad enough to do that and that situation was dealt with. It happened to be foot-and-mouth disease that came along but it could have been something else. We have handled certain cases that arose in connection with cholera and so on. Any disease in connection with animals could be dealt with.
But when you get a situation such as we had with the foot-and-mouth disease where we could not export any livestock products that were affected by the disease, that, of course, is a reasonable thing upon which to spend the money. There is more necessity for it then than there is for anything else. When the hon. member for Springfield keeps on repeating that statement with regard to the expenditure of money I am inclined to think he either does not understand the legislation or he is simply misrepresenting what the facts are to people who have not made a study of the legislation.

Mr. Speaker, this is the first time I have had the honour of speaking in this house and I am pleased to support Bill 237: an act to provide for the stabilization of the prices of agricultural commodities.
To my mind this bill is only part of an overall policy aimed at the improvement of agriculture in this country and, with the help of agricultural groups and organizations, to put it on the same level as the rest of our economy.
The success of this policy will naturally depend on the efforts of every interested group and on the way in which the law will be administered. It will not be an easy task and our best agricultural experts must take a hand in the process.
I have the honour of representing an eastern Ontario constituency where the rural population is larger than the urban population. I appreciate what the present government is doing in order to improve the lot of the farmer.
(Text):
Mr. Speaker, I first of all want to congratulate you on your elevation to the high office which you now hold. Certainly one cannot help being impressed by the dignity with which you preside over this chamber.
On this my first occasion to speak in this house, I am happy to support Bill No. 237, an act to provide for the stabilization of the
3448	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization prices of agricultural commodities. To my mind this is the beginning of a comprehensive scheme for agriculture with the co-operation of farm organizations and commodity groups, bringing agriculture into a more favourable position in our Canadian economy. The success of this measure must, of course, depend on the efforts of all groups interested in agriculture, and this legislation being intelligently applied to this objective. This is not an easy matter and it will require the best brains available, and a thorough knowledge of agriculture.
The constituency that I have the honour to represent is one of but four in southern Ontario where the rural population exceeds the urban population. I am grateful for what this government is trying to accomplish in the interests of agriculture because one of the specific promises I made was that I would do everything possible to get a better deal for agriculture. It is the privilege and the prerogative of my hon. friends across the way to criticize, but they do not take into consideration any realistic approach to this subject.
Dealing with the bill and taking beef as an example, may I say this. We must remember the two things which make for the success of this bill or the operation of it. I refer to domestic consumption in this country and our ability to export. We have increased domestic consumption of beef in the last seven years by 55 per cent. Having regard to our population of 17 million, that is a very pronounced fact. From 1948 to 1951 we had an export market in the United States. In fact, in 1950, the year of high prices, we exported one-third of the cattle produced in Canada. The reason why we export to the United States is that we have no other market in the world that will give us as high a return. It is therefore essential for us at all times to think in terms of export.
Conditions alter. The foot-and-mouth disease broke out here in the early months of 1952 and, as the former minister of agriculture has stated, we could not export beef or pork products. It was an extremely fortunate thing for this country that we had at that time the prices support act because otherwise there would have been a catastrophe. The government of the day stepped into the picture, bought this surplus beef and it did not demoralize our normal channels of trade within the coniines of our country.
But what happened in the United States? From 1953 to 1956 they have had a drought in the mid-west where one-third of their cattle population was seriously affected. When they market over 20 million cattle a year that fact has a considerable effect on the economy in this country, and our position has reversed to some extent. In 1954 we im-
TMr. Villeneuve (Glengarry-Prescott).]

ported as much beef as we exported. In 1955 and 1956 we imported into Canada more beef than we exported to the United States. This year the tide has changed. I am not saying it has changed because there is a change in government. However, the situation has changed. In the mid-west states they have had a great deal of rain this year and good growth, and they are coming to Canada to buy young cattle with which to restock and replenish those farms which had to get rid of those cattle. The result has been that this year we have exported over 10 per cent of our production of cattle which makes a very significant difference. Therefore the price and the future for the beef producer looks very bright.
I do not want the western farmer, particularly the wheat grower to think that this bill is designed merely to help the eastern farmer since it is not specifically dealing with benefits to him. However, 65 per cent of the cattle produced in Canada does come from the four prairie provinces where we have only 27 per cent of the population. That surplus has to be moved to the eastern section of the country or to the United States. Therefore I say the government's legislation is designed, having in mind the overall picture, to help production throughout all regions in this country.
Dealing with pork, there is of course disease among United States hogs and a bill has been passed through this parliament prohibiting the importation of hogs from the United States. We have been favoured with very substantial returns because of the prohibition of importation of United States hogs since 1952, with the exception of course of the year 1955. Those people raise an average of from 60 to 65 million hogs a year, while we in Canada raise somewhere between 5 and 6 million. Yet, as I have said, this prohibition has had a very pronounced bearing on the situation. My friends across the way do not realize that we have a reciprocal trade arrangement where items must flow both ways. A lot of these things must be faced in a realistic manner and we must appraise the situation as it affects the whole North American continent and not just take a slant such as "Here I am and I am entitled to more money." We all feel that, but I believe that looking back 10 years you do get some of the largest returns we have had, although in the last three years certain items have been somewhat depressed. For example, the cattle situation which has been affected by the United States not importing as many cattle as they normally would have done. Nevertheless you have a fair average.

We are confronted with another serious problem about which I truthfully state I do not know what we can do. In western Ontario I know of at least 10 men who feed as many as 1,000 cattle in a year and anyone knows that such a man does not need the same return required by the ordinary small farmer-that is to say on the basis of the percentage per head profit-in order to make a success of his business. In Brampton, as the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Pallett) knows, one man alone in 1956 raised 90,000 turkeys; this year it is up to 130,000. Farmer after farmer in my own area who used to produce 300 to 500 turkeys found he was getting such a small margin of profit and the danger of loss was so great that he eventually had to abolish that part of his business altogether.
I ask how are you going to arrive at parity prices? Are you going to take the successful big operator or are you going to take the deficient farmer? To get a fair return for any of these people it is not easy; it is quite all right to criticize but it is not easy. I think this bill is at least an approach to the problem. I do not say it is everything it should be-I would be the last one to say that-but at least it is a sound approach.
One thing I like about this Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) is that he does not go up and down the country like the former minister of agriculture, telling the farmers how well off they are. Eighty-five per cent of the population of Canada are consumers who perhaps do not understand the agricultural picture. I say that our minister is conscientious and he is doing the very best he can and does not go around saying that everything is rosy in agriculture when it is not.

continue, Mr. Speaker, in the years since 1941 my constituency has produced more cheese
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization than any other constituency in Canada and naturally I am vitally interested in that commodity. In the period from 1941 to 1949 the government of the day, because of the effects of war and those of the postwar period, requisitioned all the cheese in Canada for shipment to Britain at a fixed price. I am not critical of that; it was a situation which any government would have had to meet and look after, but from 1948 on in the province of Ontario we have had what is known as the dairy herd improvement plan under which 1,186 herds of dairy cattle last year were put under test to establish the costs of production of milk in various areas under various conditions.

In 1950 as a result of inquiries made under this dairy herd improvement plan milk production was found to be $3 per hundred or thereabouts, that is to say in cheese producing areas. In fluid milk areas naturally the cost is more but that is a different problem.
There was a great clamour in the province for marketing boards and farmers wanted to set up their own selling agencies to look after the interests of the people they represented. Therefore 18 different types of marketing organizations for farmers and producers were set up in the province of Ontario; the cheese producers association was one. They sold their cheese at 28 cents in 1950. In 1951 the then minister of agriculture, under this prices support act, stated that 28 cents was the guaranteed price. Three of these gentlemen who went to Great Britain tried to get a better return for the producers they represented in this association. They may have made a mistake in that they did not go to the Department of Agriculture of the federal government to state the facts of their case because I am sure the then minister of agriculture would have been very happy to go along with their requests to better their conditions. They were, however, fortunate enough to be able to sell their cheese in Britain at 32 cents. In 1951 the province of Ontario established a fixed price for that board of 36 cents. It amounted altogether to something in the neighbourhood of $3 in net return to the producers, which of course was the object in the first place.
Now what happened? Eight times more New Zealand cheese was allowed to come into this country in the years 1950, 1951 and 1952 than had been imported for 40 years previously, and when asked about it in this

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization house the government of that day said nothing could be done to stop it. The result was that we in the cheese industry have never got back the cost of production, much as we have tried. This year they have got the price up to 34 cents, but the province of Ontario has paid guarantees for the last ten cents a pound amounting to a million and a half to keep that industry up. The first 24 cents is guaranteed under the co-operative plan as designed by the government. I am not finding fault there, because they can only lend up to 80 per cent of the three year average, but the producers are still far from getting a fair deal.
I happen to have an extract here which relates to this question. The hon. member for Middlesex East (Mr. White) asked this question on Monday, January 10, 1955 about the import of cheese, as recorded in Hansard at page 20:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture. Does the minister plan to make any change in the regulations that now permit the importation of New Zealand cheese when there is a surplus of cheese and other dairy products in Canada?
In reply, the Eight Hon. C. D. Howe, minister of trade and commerce said:
Mr. Speaker, there is no prohibition on the importing of cheese. There is a duty on cheese, and technically anyone can ship cheese into Canada who can do so over the duty. A verbal arrangement was made with New Zealand at a time when we were having difficulty exporting to the British market. New Zealand was asked not to ship cheese to this market. The circumstances under which the request was made have changed. New Zealand was pressing to be relieved from that verbal agreement and there seemed no very good ground for insisting that it be continued. The shipment of cheese has been made in the ordinary course of business in the same way that anything else is exported to Canada. I suggest it is a mistake to say that we allowed the import. The normal laws of the land were allowed to function in this matter.
The former minister of agriculture, the right hon. member for Melville, later stated:
In order that there will be no misunderstanding I want it completely understood that I fully agree with what the Department of Trade and Commerce did.
And, later:
I was merely drawing attention to the fact that the hon. member who asked the question did not ask it of the right minister. I did not know exactly what might have been in his mind, so I thought it was necessary to say what I did.
Mr. Speaker, I say this does not sound exactly the same as the statement which the former minister of trade and commerce (Mr. Howe) made in May of last year when he said there would be no more importation of New Zealand cheese for the next 12 months, four weeks before the federal election.

speechtext: There had been a different agreement entered into a year before that.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
One
must understand, Mr. Speaker, that this cheese comes in at one cent a pound and the only agreement I know of is one which the province of Ontario made with the minister of trade and commerce of that day stating Ontario's position that it was willing to make guarantees to the cheese marketing board on one condition, namely that no importation of New Zealand cheese would come into Canada while we had a surplus on hand.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: And the Department of Trade and Commerce made an agreement with New Zealand that they would not send cheese here without a permit from the government.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
That is right. I am glad we agree on some things. Mr. Speaker, I do not want to take a selfish attitude because dairying affects every province across this land. But the unfortunate dairyman who has no fluid milk market in this country has been up against it, and to my mind I do not see why, because we have only approximately 2 per cent of surplus on dairy products in Canada, yet our farmers who have to produce milk to go into processing whether it is powdered milk, canned milk or butter, have had to produce at a loss ever since this price has been established. I do not think the dairy industry alone should sustain this loss, and I will say right now that the way to overcome it is not by means of a hit or miss policy such as has been adopted in the past with regard to cost of production, but by trying to give the producer a reasonable rate of return. If the producer had $3 a hundred-and that is not an exorbitant price when you consider that fluid milk sells at $4.80 or thereabouts-he would be reasonably happy.
The net return to farmers in the area from which I come was $2.73 a hundred, and on the basis of this dairy herd improvement plan which has been in operation for 10 years the cost of producing the milk was $3.06 a hundred. I do not believe any man, and particularly any man in the dairy industry, would consider that only 2 per cent of overall surplus production cannot be controlled in order to give the producers a fair return.
As far as sheep are concerned I do not want to be personal. There is only one man I know of who made money out of sheep in this country, and that was the gentleman from Alberta who had the good fortune to have disease in his flock and got $150 a head for them. I have sold quite a few at four cents to eleven cents a pound in the last five years

in the Montreal market, average weights 125 to 150 pounds; lambs from 17 cents to 22 cents. So this still gives me the idea that if you are a good friend of certain people you are certainly well compensated for your crop.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: I wonder if the hon. member remembers the statement he made the last time he and I were on the same platform?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, at the end I said I made a little mistake in reading figures. But I will tell you more about cheese. In ten years you have given the cheese industry of Canada under the price support act $155,348.82. You gave one farmer $150 a head for losing his sheep, which was ten times more than the market value, at least.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Nobody who knows anything about it agrees with you, but that does not matter. Go right along.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Just a minute, and I will tell you something. In 1952 when the foot-and-mouth disease broke out the province of Ontario came to the rescue of the producers and particularly the cheese industry. It provided $293,000 out of the treasury. This was money that had not been voted. It was given in the form of price supports such as we have here. This had to be taken from the provincial department of agriculture. That is the treatment the cheese producers received under you, as minister of agriculture.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Tell them what we did the night we went down with you.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, I know one thing you did. The floor price was around 25 cents on cheese and there was no sale for it. The next morning you and the then hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Chevrier) made an announcement. I think he persuaded you to do it because he knew the temperament of the producers and the feeling that prevailed that night. You gave us a 30-cent guarantee.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: We did no such thing. We bought 500,000 pounds of cheese at 30 cents.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: What about your present Minister of Agriculture?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
It is
quite easy to criticize and that is our privilege in a democracy. On the other hand I am the first one to admit that this problem is not an easy one to solve and I will say this. Though I may have strong differences of opinion with the hon. member for Melville I readily recognize that he is a man with an iron-clad constitution because he has 96698-219
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization been able to hold the portfolio of minister of agriculture of this country for 22 years. I will admit that.
My hon. friends opposite have offered a lot of remedies for the present agricultural situation but they have not come out with any constructive criticism or suggestion with regard to the bill before us. As I stated previously, I have every confidence that the farmers and producers will receive a fair deal under this legislation because it has a ten-year basis even with respect to dairy products. Subclause 2 of clause 2 of the bill reads as follows:
(2) In prescribing a percentage of the base price of an agricultural commodity under subparagraph (i) or (ii) of paragraph (e) of subsection (1). the governor in council shall have regard to the estimated average cost of production of the commodity, and such other factors as the governor in council considers to be relevant.
The advisory committee will be composed of from six to nine members representing farm organizations and commodity groups across this land. These people will be in contact with producers at all times. I am firmly convinced that we have every reason to expect this bill, if intelligently applied, will be the most advanced piece of farm legislation to have been enacted by this house in the past 25 years.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to have this opportunity of supporting the amendment moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. McCullough) to the effect that this legislation should be referred to the committee of this house on agriculture and colonization. However, before dealing with the measure before us this evening I should like to comment briefly on one or two of the statements that were made in this house this evening by hon. members opposite. I should like to refer in the first instance to the speech made by the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Gardiner). I have always had a great deal of admiration for the debating ability of the hon. member for Melville when he hits above the belt but the personal attack that we heard him make this evening against the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Schulz), employing tactics of smear and innuendo, represents the kind of intimidation for which the hon. member is so well known. That is the reason why we in the province of Saskatchewan grew so tired of the hon. member's personal vendettas and kicked him and his government out in 1944 and the Liberal party in that province has been as dead as Nebuchadnezzar's aunt ever since.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.

Mr. Speaker, may I point out that the hon. gentleman has forgotten his

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: You control the machine out there along with everything else.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the blame for the defeat of the Liberal party in the last federal election can in large measure be laid on the doorstep of the hon. member for Melville in so far as the defeat of western Liberal candidates is concerned. I made no attack. I simply read what the hon. member said himself. That is all.
